text:
Heatmaps visualise data through variations in colouring. When applied to a tabular format, heatmaps are useful for cross-examining multivariate data, through placing variables in the columns and observation (or records) in rows and colouring the cells within the table. Heatmaps are good for showing variance across multiple variables, revealing any patterns, displaying whether any variables are similar to each other, and for detecting if any correlations exist in-between them.
In this hands-on exercise, you will gain hands-on experience on using R to plot static and interactive heatmap for visualising and analysing multivariate data.




pacman::p_load(seriation, dendextend, heatmaply, tidyverse)


The downloaded binary packages are in
    /var/folders/ry/c12ynh2n3lvc78fj89rgdbtw0000gn/T//RtmphFkIVG/downloaded_packages



The downloaded binary packages are in
    /var/folders/ry/c12ynh2n3lvc78fj89rgdbtw0000gn/T//RtmphFkIVG/downloaded_packages



The downloaded binary packages are in
    /var/folders/ry/c12ynh2n3lvc78fj89rgdbtw0000gn/T//RtmphFkIVG/downloaded_packages







In this hands-on exercise, the data of World Happiness 2018 report will be used.




wh <- read_csv("../data/WHData-2018.csv")





row.names(wh) <- wh$Country




The data was loaded into a data frame, but it has to be a data matrix to make your heatmap.

wh1 <- dplyr::select(wh, c(3, 7:12))
wh_matrix <- data.matrix(wh)

Notice that wh_matrix is in R matrix format.







wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix,
                      Rowv=NA, Colv=NA)














Note



By default, heatmap() plots a cluster heatmap. The arguments Rowv=NA and Colv=NA are used to switch off the option of plotting the row and column dendrograms. To plot a cluster heatmap, we just have to use the default as shown in the code chunk below.



wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix)














Note



The order of both rows and columns is different compared to the native wh_matrix. This is because heatmap does a reordering using clusterisation: it calculates the distance between each pair of rows and columns and tries to order them by similarity. Moreover, the corresponding dendrogram are provided beside the heatmap.
Here, red cells denote small values. This heatmap is not really informative because the Happiness Score variable has relatively higher values, making the other variables with small values all look the same. Thus, we need to normalize this matrix using the scale argument.


The code chunk below normalises the matrix column-wise.

wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix,
                      scale="column",
                      cexRow = 0.6,
                      cexCol = 0.8,
                      margins = c(10, 4))








Notice that the values are scaled now. Also note that margins argument is used to ensure that the entire x-axis labels are displayed completely and, cexRow and cexCol arguments are used to define the font size used for y-axis and x-axis labels respectively.




heatmaply is an R package for building interactive cluster heatmap that can be shared online as a stand-alone HTML file. It is designed and maintained by Tal Galili.
In this section, you will gain hands-on experience on using heatmaply to design an interactive cluster heatmap. We will still use the wh_matrix as the input data.



heatmaply(mtcars)





The code chunk below shows the basic syntax needed to create an interactive heatmap by using heatmaply package.

heatmaply(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)])











Note




Different from heatmap(), for heatmaply() the default horizontal dendrogram is placed on the left hand side of the heatmap.
The text label of each row, on the other hand, is placed on the right hand side of the heat map.
When the x-axis marker labels are too long, they will be rotated by 135 degree from the north.






When analysing multivariate data set, it is very common that the variables in the data sets includes values that reflect different types of measurement. In order to ensure that all the variables have comparable values, data transformation are commonly used before clustering.
Three main data transformation methods are supported by heatmaply(), namely: scale, normalise and percentilse.


When all variables are came from or assumed to come from some normal distribution, then scaling (i.e.: subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation) would bring them all close to the standard normal distribution. In such a case, each value would reflect the distance from the mean in units of standard deviation. The scale argument in heatmaply() supports column and row scaling.

heatmaply(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)],
          scale = "column")








When variables in the data comes from possibly different (and non-normal) distributions, the normalize function can be used to bring data to the 0 to 1 scale by subtracting the minimum and dividing by the maximum of all observations. This preserves the shape of each variable’s distribution while making them easily comparable on the same “scale”. Different from Scaling, the normalise method is performed on the input data set i.e. wh_matrix as shown in the code chunk below.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]))








This is similar to ranking the variables, but instead of keeping the rank values, divide them by the maximal rank. This is done by using the ecdf of the variables on their own values, bringing each value to its empirical percentile. The benefit of the percentize function is that each value has a relatively clear interpretation, it is the percent of observations that got that value or below it. Similar to Normalize method, the Percentize method is also performed on the input data set i.e. wh_matrix as shown in the code chunk below.

heatmaply(percentize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]))









heatmaply supports a variety of hierarchical clustering algorithm. The main arguments provided are:

distfun: function used to compute the distance (dissimilarity) between both rows and columns. Defaults to dist. The options "pearson", "spearman" and "kendall" can be used to use correlation-based clustering, which uses as.dist(1 - cor(t(x))) as the distance metric.
hclustfun: function used to compute the hierarchical clustering when Rowv or Colv are not dendrograms. Defaults to hclust.
dist_method: default is NULL, which results in "euclidean" to be used. It can accept alternative character strings indicating the method to be passed to distfun. By default distfun is "dist" hence this can be one of "euclidean", "maximum", "manhattan", "canberra", "binary" or "minkowski".
hclust_method: default is NULL, which results in "complete" method to be used. It can accept alternative character strings indicating the method to be passed to hclustfun. By default hclustfun is hclust hence this can be one of "ward.D", "ward.D2", "single", "complete", "average" (= UPGMA), "mcquitty" (= WPGMA), "median" (= WPGMC) or "centroid" (= UPGMC).

In general, a clustering model can be calibrated either manually or statistically.



In the code chunk below, the heatmap is plotted by using hierarchical clustering algorithm with “Euclidean distance” and “ward.D” method.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "ward.D")








In order to determine the best clustering method and number of cluster the dend_expend() and find_k() functions of dendextend package will be used.
First, the dend_expend() will be used to determine the recommended clustering method to be used.

wh_d <- dist(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]), method = "euclidean")
dend_expend(wh_d)[[3]]

  dist_methods hclust_methods     optim
1      unknown         ward.D 0.6137851
2      unknown        ward.D2 0.6289186
3      unknown         single 0.4774362
4      unknown       complete 0.6434009
5      unknown        average 0.6701688
6      unknown       mcquitty 0.5020102
7      unknown         median 0.5901833
8      unknown       centroid 0.6338734


The output table shows that “average” method should be used because it gave the high optimum value.
Next, find_k() is used to determine the optimal number of cluster.

wh_clust <- hclust(wh_d, method = "average")
num_k <- find_k(wh_clust)
plot(num_k)








Figure above shows that k=3 would be good.
With reference to the statistical analysis results, we can prepare the code chunk as shown below.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "average",
          k_row = 3)








One of the problems with hierarchical clustering is that it doesn’t actually place the rows in a definite order, it merely constrains the space of possible orderings. heatmaply uses the seriation package to find an optimal ordering of rows and columns. Optimal means to optimize the Hamiltonian path length that is restricted by the dendrogram structure. This, in other words, means to rotate the branches so that the sum of distances between each adjacent leaf (label) will be minimized.
Here we meet our first seriation algorithm: Optimal Leaf Ordering (OLO). This algorithm starts with the output of an agglomerative clustering algorithm and produces a unique ordering, one that flips the various branches of the dendrogram around so as to minimize the sum of dissimilarities between adjacent leaves.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "OLO")





The default options is "OLO" (Optimal leaf ordering) which optimizes the above criterion (in O(n^4)). Another option is "GW" (Gruvaeus and Wainer) which aims for the same goal but uses a potentially faster heuristic.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "GW")





The option "mean" gives the output we would get by default from heatmap functions in other packages such as gplots::heatmap.2.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "mean")





The option "none" gives us the dendrograms without any rotation that is based on the data matrix.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "none")








The default colour palette used by heatmaply is viridis. heatmaply users, however, can use other colour palettes in order to improve the aestheticness and visual friendliness of the heatmap.
In the code chunk below, the Blues colour palette of rColorBrewer is used.

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          seriate = "none",
          colors = Blues)








Beside providing a wide collection of arguments for meeting the statistical analysis needs, heatmaply also provides many plotting features to ensure cartographic quality heatmap can be produced.
In the code chunk below the following arguments are used:

k_row is used to produce 5 groups.
margins is used to change the top margin to 60 and row margin to 200.
fontsize_row and fontsize_col are used to change the font size for row and column labels to 4.
main is used to write the main title of the plot.
xlab and ylab are used to write the x-axis and y-axis labels respectively.


heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          Colv=NA,
          seriate = "none",
          colors = Blues,
          k_row = 5,
          margins = c(NA,200,60,NA),
          fontsize_row = 4,
          fontsize_col = 5,
          main="World Happiness Score and Variables by Country, 2018 \nData Transformation using Normalise Method",
          xlab = "World Happiness Indicators",
          ylab = "World Countries"
          )

text:
Heatmaps visualise data through variations in colouring. When applied to a tabular format, heatmaps are useful for cross-examining multivariate data, through placing variables in the columns and observation (or records) in rows and colouring the cells within the table. Heatmaps are good for showing variance across multiple variables, revealing any patterns, displaying whether any variables are similar to each other, and for detecting if any correlations exist in-between them.
In this hands-on exercise, you will gain hands-on experience on using R to plot static and interactive heatmap for visualising and analysing multivariate data.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 (Part 5)
text:
In this hands-on exercise, you will gain hands-on experiences on designing treemap using appropriate R packages. The hands-on exercise consists of three main section. First, you will learn how to manipulate transaction data into a treemap strcuture by using selected functions provided in dplyr package. Then, you will learn how to plot static treemap by using treemap package. In the third section, you will learn how to design interactive treemap by using d3treeR package.




pacman::p_load(treemap, treemapify, tidyverse) 






In this exercise, REALIS2018.csv data will be used. This dataset provides information of private property transaction records in 2018. The dataset is extracted from REALIS portal (https://spring.ura.gov.sg/lad/ore/login/index.cfm) of Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA).




realis2018 <- read_csv("../data/realis2018.csv")




The data.frame realis2018 is in transaction record form, which is highly disaggregated and not appropriate to be used to plot a treemap. In this section, we will perform the following steps to manipulate and prepare a data.frame that is appropriate for treemap visualisation:

Group transaction records by Project Name, Planning Region, Planning Area, Property Type and Type of Sale, and
Compute Total Unit Sold, Total Area, Median Unit Price and Median Transacted Price by applying appropriate summary statistics on No. of Units, Area (sqm), Unit Price ($ psm) and Transacted Price ($) respectively.

Two key verbs of dplyr package, namely: group_by() and summarize() will be used to perform these steps.
group_by() breaks down a data.frame into specified groups of rows. When you then apply the verbs above on the resulting object they’ll be automatically applied “by group”.
Grouping affects the verbs as follows:

grouped select() is the same as ungrouped select(), except that grouping variables are always retained.
grouped arrange() is the same as ungrouped; unless you set .by_group = TRUE, in which case it orders first by the grouping variables.
mutate() and filter() are most useful in conjunction with window functions (like rank(), or min(x) == x).
sample_n() and sample_frac() sample the specified number/fraction of rows in each group.
summarise() computes the summary for each group.

In our case, group_by() will be used together with summarise() to derive the summarised data.frame.



The code chank below shows a typical two lines code approach to perform the steps.

realis2018_grouped <- group_by(realis2018, `Project Name`,
                               `Planning Region`, `Planning Area`, 
                               `Property Type`, `Type of Sale`)
realis2018_summarised <- summarise(realis2018_grouped, 
                          `Total Unit Sold` = sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE),
                          `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
                          `Median Unit Price ($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE), 
                          `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE))

The code chunk above is not very efficient because we have to give each intermediate data.frame a name, even though we don’t have to care about it.



The code chunk below shows a more efficient way to tackle the same processes by using the pipe, %>%:

realis2018_summarised <- realis2018 %>% 
  group_by(`Project Name`,`Planning Region`, 
           `Planning Area`, `Property Type`, 
           `Type of Sale`) %>%
  summarise(`Total Unit Sold` = sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE), 
            `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Median Unit Price ($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE))





treemap package is a R package specially designed to offer great flexibility in drawing treemaps. The core function, namely: treemap() offers at least 43 arguments. In this section, we will only explore the major arguments for designing elegant and yet truthful treemaps.


In this section, treemap() of Treemap package is used to plot a treemap showing the distribution of median unit prices and total unit sold of resale condominium by geographic hierarchy in 2017.
First, we will select records belongs to resale condominium property type from realis2018_selected data frame.

realis2018_selected <- realis2018_summarised %>%
  filter(`Property Type` == "Condominium", `Type of Sale` == "Resale")




The code chunk below designed a treemap by using three core arguments of treemap(), namely: index, vSize and vColor.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )








Things to learn from the three arguments used:

index: The index vector must consist of at least two column names or else no hierarchy treemap will be plotted. If multiple column names are provided, the first name is the highest aggregation level, the second name the second highest aggregation level, and so on.
vSize: The column must not contain negative values. This is because its values will be used to map the sizes of the rectangles of the treemaps.







Warning



The treemap above was wrongly coloured. For a correctly designed treemap, the colours of the rectangles should be in different intensity showing, in our case, median unit prices.
For treemap(), vColor is used in combination with the argument type to determine the colours of the rectangles. Without defining type, like the code chunk above, treemap() assumes type = index, in our case, the hierarchy of planning areas.





In the code chunk below, type argument is defined as value.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type = "value",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )








Things to learn from the code chunk above:

The rectangles are coloured with different intensity of green, reflecting their respective median unit prices.
The legend reveals that the values are binned into ten bins, i.e. 0-5000, 5000-10000, etc. with an equal interval of 5000.




There are two arguments that determine the mapping to color palettes: mapping and palette. The only difference between “value” and “manual” is the default value for mapping. The “value” treemap considers palette to be a diverging color palette (say ColorBrewer’s “RdYlBu”), and maps it in such a way that 0 corresponds to the middle color (typically white or yellow), -max(abs(values)) to the left-end color, and max(abs(values)), to the right-end color. The “manual” treemap simply maps min(values) to the left-end color, max(values) to the right-end color, and mean(range(values)) to the middle color.




treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="value",
        palette="RdYlBu", 
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )








Things to learn from the code chunk above:

Although the colour palette used is RdYlBu but there are no red rectangles in the treemap above. This is because all the median unit prices are positive.
The reason why we see only 5000 to 45000 in the legend is because the range argument is by default c(min(values), max(values)) with some pretty rounding.




The “manual” type does not interpret the values as the “value” type does. Instead, the value range is mapped linearly to the colour palette.
The code chunk below shows a manual type treemap.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="RdYlBu", 
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )








Things to learn from the code chunk above:

The colour scheme used is very confusing. This is because mapping = (min(values), mean(range(values)), max(values)). It is not wise to use diverging colour palette such as RdYlBu if the values are all positive or negative.
To overcome this problem, a single colour palette such as Blues should be used.


treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="Blues",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )











treemap() supports two popular treemap layouts, namely: ”squarified” and ”pivotSize”. The default is ”pivotSize”.
The squarified treemap algorithm (Bruls et al., 2000) produces good aspect ratios, but ignores the sorting order of the rectangles (sortID). The ordered treemap, pivot-by-size, algorithm (Bederson et al., 2002) takes the sorting order (sortID) into account while aspect ratios are still acceptable.



The code chunk below plots a squarified treemap by changing the algorithm argument.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="Blues", 
        algorithm = "squarified",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )











When ”pivotSize” algorithm is used, sortID argument can be used to determine the order in which the rectangles are placed from top left to bottom right.

        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="Blues", 
        algorithm = "pivotSize",
        sortID = "Median Transacted Price",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )












treemapify is a R package specially developed to draw treemaps in ggplot2. In this section, you will learn how to design treemaps closely resembling treemaps designed in the previous section by using treemapify. Before you get started, you should read the Introduction to “treemapify” and its user guide.

           fill = `Median Unit Price ($ psm)`,

           subgroup2 = `Planning Area`)) +

Adding boundary line

ggplot(data=realis2018_selected,
       aes(area = `Total Unit Sold`,
           fill = `Median Unit Price ($ psm)`,
           subgroup = `Planning Region`,
           subgroup2 = `Planning Area`)) +
  geom_treemap() +
  geom_treemap_subgroup2_border(colour = "gray40",
                                size = 2) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_border(colour = "gray20")

text: In this hands-on exercise, you will gain hands-on experiences on designing treemap using appropriate R packages. The hands-on exercise consists of three main section. First, you will learn how to manipulate transaction data into a treemap strcuture by using selected functions provided in dplyr package. Then, you will learn how to plot static treemap by using treemap package. In the third section, you will learn how to design interactive treemap by using d3treeR package.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 (Part 5)
text: pacman::p_load(treemap, treemapify, tidyverse)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 (Part 5)
text:
In this exercise, REALIS2018.csv data will be used. This dataset provides information of private property transaction records in 2018. The dataset is extracted from REALIS portal (https://spring.ura.gov.sg/lad/ore/login/index.cfm) of Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA).




realis2018 <- read_csv("../data/realis2018.csv")




The data.frame realis2018 is in transaction record form, which is highly disaggregated and not appropriate to be used to plot a treemap. In this section, we will perform the following steps to manipulate and prepare a data.frame that is appropriate for treemap visualisation:

Group transaction records by Project Name, Planning Region, Planning Area, Property Type and Type of Sale, and
Compute Total Unit Sold, Total Area, Median Unit Price and Median Transacted Price by applying appropriate summary statistics on No. of Units, Area (sqm), Unit Price ($ psm) and Transacted Price ($) respectively.

Two key verbs of dplyr package, namely: group_by() and summarize() will be used to perform these steps.
group_by() breaks down a data.frame into specified groups of rows. When you then apply the verbs above on the resulting object they’ll be automatically applied “by group”.
Grouping affects the verbs as follows:

grouped select() is the same as ungrouped select(), except that grouping variables are always retained.
grouped arrange() is the same as ungrouped; unless you set .by_group = TRUE, in which case it orders first by the grouping variables.
mutate() and filter() are most useful in conjunction with window functions (like rank(), or min(x) == x).
sample_n() and sample_frac() sample the specified number/fraction of rows in each group.
summarise() computes the summary for each group.

In our case, group_by() will be used together with summarise() to derive the summarised data.frame.



The code chank below shows a typical two lines code approach to perform the steps.

realis2018_grouped <- group_by(realis2018, `Project Name`,
                               `Planning Region`, `Planning Area`, 
                               `Property Type`, `Type of Sale`)
realis2018_summarised <- summarise(realis2018_grouped, 
                          `Total Unit Sold` = sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE),
                          `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
                          `Median Unit Price ($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE), 
                          `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE))

The code chunk above is not very efficient because we have to give each intermediate data.frame a name, even though we don’t have to care about it.



The code chunk below shows a more efficient way to tackle the same processes by using the pipe, %>%:

realis2018_summarised <- realis2018 %>% 
  group_by(`Project Name`,`Planning Region`, 
           `Planning Area`, `Property Type`, 
           `Type of Sale`) %>%
  summarise(`Total Unit Sold` = sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE), 
            `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Median Unit Price ($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE))

title: Hands-on Exercise 5 (Part 5)
text:
treemap package is a R package specially designed to offer great flexibility in drawing treemaps. The core function, namely: treemap() offers at least 43 arguments. In this section, we will only explore the major arguments for designing elegant and yet truthful treemaps.


In this section, treemap() of Treemap package is used to plot a treemap showing the distribution of median unit prices and total unit sold of resale condominium by geographic hierarchy in 2017.
First, we will select records belongs to resale condominium property type from realis2018_selected data frame.

realis2018_selected <- realis2018_summarised %>%
  filter(`Property Type` == "Condominium", `Type of Sale` == "Resale")




The code chunk below designed a treemap by using three core arguments of treemap(), namely: index, vSize and vColor.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )








Things to learn from the three arguments used:

index: The index vector must consist of at least two column names or else no hierarchy treemap will be plotted. If multiple column names are provided, the first name is the highest aggregation level, the second name the second highest aggregation level, and so on.
vSize: The column must not contain negative values. This is because its values will be used to map the sizes of the rectangles of the treemaps.







Warning



The treemap above was wrongly coloured. For a correctly designed treemap, the colours of the rectangles should be in different intensity showing, in our case, median unit prices.
For treemap(), vColor is used in combination with the argument type to determine the colours of the rectangles. Without defining type, like the code chunk above, treemap() assumes type = index, in our case, the hierarchy of planning areas.





In the code chunk below, type argument is defined as value.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type = "value",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )








Things to learn from the code chunk above:

The rectangles are coloured with different intensity of green, reflecting their respective median unit prices.
The legend reveals that the values are binned into ten bins, i.e. 0-5000, 5000-10000, etc. with an equal interval of 5000.




There are two arguments that determine the mapping to color palettes: mapping and palette. The only difference between “value” and “manual” is the default value for mapping. The “value” treemap considers palette to be a diverging color palette (say ColorBrewer’s “RdYlBu”), and maps it in such a way that 0 corresponds to the middle color (typically white or yellow), -max(abs(values)) to the left-end color, and max(abs(values)), to the right-end color. The “manual” treemap simply maps min(values) to the left-end color, max(values) to the right-end color, and mean(range(values)) to the middle color.




treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="value",
        palette="RdYlBu", 
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )








Things to learn from the code chunk above:

Although the colour palette used is RdYlBu but there are no red rectangles in the treemap above. This is because all the median unit prices are positive.
The reason why we see only 5000 to 45000 in the legend is because the range argument is by default c(min(values), max(values)) with some pretty rounding.




The “manual” type does not interpret the values as the “value” type does. Instead, the value range is mapped linearly to the colour palette.
The code chunk below shows a manual type treemap.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="RdYlBu", 
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )








Things to learn from the code chunk above:

The colour scheme used is very confusing. This is because mapping = (min(values), mean(range(values)), max(values)). It is not wise to use diverging colour palette such as RdYlBu if the values are all positive or negative.
To overcome this problem, a single colour palette such as Blues should be used.


treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="Blues",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )











treemap() supports two popular treemap layouts, namely: ”squarified” and ”pivotSize”. The default is ”pivotSize”.
The squarified treemap algorithm (Bruls et al., 2000) produces good aspect ratios, but ignores the sorting order of the rectangles (sortID). The ordered treemap, pivot-by-size, algorithm (Bederson et al., 2002) takes the sorting order (sortID) into account while aspect ratios are still acceptable.



The code chunk below plots a squarified treemap by changing the algorithm argument.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="Blues", 
        algorithm = "squarified",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )











When ”pivotSize” algorithm is used, sortID argument can be used to determine the order in which the rectangles are placed from top left to bottom right.

treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="Blues", 
        algorithm = "pivotSize",
        sortID = "Median Transacted Price",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )

title: Hands-on Exercise 7 (Part 2)
text:
In this hands-on exercise, you will learn how to visualise and analyse text data using R.
By the end of this hands-on exercise, you will be able to:

understand tidytext framework for processing, analysing and visualising text data,
write function for importing multiple files into R,
combine multiple files into a single data frame,
clean and wrangle text data by using tidyverse approach,
visualise words with Word Cloud,
compute term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) using tidytext method, and
visualise texts and terms relationships.





In this hands-on exercise, the following R packages for handling, processing, wrangling, analysing and visualising text data will be used:

tidytext, tidyverse (mainly readr, purrr, stringr, ggplot2)
widyr,
wordcloud and ggwordcloud,
textplot (requires igraph, tidygraph and ggraph)
DT,
lubridate and hms.


pacman::p_load(tidytext, widyr, wordcloud, DT, ggwordcloud, textplot, lubridate, hms,
               tidyverse, tidygraph, ggraph, igraph)








news20 <- "../data/20news/"





read_folder <- function(infolder) {
  tibble(file = dir(infolder,
                    full.names = TRUE)) %>%
    mutate(text = map(file,
                      read_lines)) %>%
    transmute(id = basename(file),
              text) %>%
    unnest(text)
}





raw_text <- tibble(folder =
                     dir(news20,
                         full.names = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(folder_out = map(folder,
                          read_folder)) %>%
  unnest(cols = c(folder_out)) %>%
  transmute(newsgroup = basename(folder),
            id, text)
#write_rds(raw_text, "../data/rds/news20.rds")






raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  summarize(messages = n_distinct(id)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(messages, newsgroup)) +
  geom_col(fill = 'lightblue') +
  labs(y = NULL)











Using tidy data principles in processing, analysing and visualising text data. Much of the infrastructure needed for text mining with tidy data frames already exists in packages like ‘dplyr’, ‘broom’, ‘tidyr’, and ‘ggplot2’.
Figure below shows the workflow using tidytext approach for processing and visualising text data:
Text Data → (unnest_tokens tidytext) → Tidy Text (dplyr, tidyr) → (count dplyr) → Summarized Text (dplyr, tidyr) → (ggplot2) → Visualizations


Notice that each message has some structure and extra text that we don’t want to include in our analysis. For example, every message has a header, containing fields such as “from:” or “in_reply_to:” that describe the message. Some also have automated email signatures, which occur after a line like “–“.

cleaned_text <- raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup, id) %>%
  filter(cumsum(text == "") > 0,
         cumsum(str_detect(
           text, "^--")) == 0) %>%
  ungroup()

Things to learn from the code chunk above:

cumsum() of base R is used to return a vector whose elements are the cumulative sums of the elements of the argument.
str_detect() from stringr is used to detect the presence or absence of a pattern in a string.




In this code chunk below, regular expressions are used to remove lines with nested text representing quotes from other users.

cleaned_text <- cleaned_text %>%
  filter(str_detect(text, "^[^>]+[A-Za-z\\d]")
         | text == "",
         !str_detect(text,
                     "writes(:|\\.\\.\\.)$"),
         !str_detect(text,
                     "^In article <")
  )

Things to learn from the code chunk above:

str_detect() from stringr is used to detect the presence or absence of a pattern in a string.
filter() of dplyr package is used to subset a data frame, retaining all rows that satisfy the specified conditions.




In this code chunk below, unnest_tokens() of tidytext package is used to split the dataset into tokens, while stop_words() is used to remove stop-words.

usenet_words <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  filter(str_detect(word, "[a-z’]$"),
         !word %in% stop_words$word)

Now that we’ve removed the headers, signatures, and formatting, we can start exploring common words. For starters, we could find the most common words in the entire dataset, or within particular newsgroups.

usenet_words %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE)

# A tibble: 5,542 × 2
   word           n
   <chr>      <int>
 1 people        57
 2 time          50
 3 jesus         47
 4 god           44
 5 message       40
 6 br            27
 7 bible         23
 8 drive         23
 9 homosexual    23
10 read          22
# ℹ 5,532 more rows


Instead of counting individual words, you can also count words within by newsgroup by using the code chunk below.

words_by_newsgroup <- usenet_words %>%
  count(newsgroup, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  ungroup()




In this code chunk below, wordcloud() of wordcloud package is used to plot a static wordcloud.

wordcloud(words_by_newsgroup$word,
          words_by_newsgroup$n,
          max.words = 300)








A DT table can be used to complement the visual discovery.
The wordcloud below is plotted by using ggwordcloud package.

set.seed(1234)

words_by_newsgroup %>%
  filter(n > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(label = word,
             size = n)) +
  geom_text_wordcloud() +
  theme_minimal() +
  facet_wrap(~newsgroup)












tf–idf, short for term frequency–inverse document frequency, is a numerical statistic that is intended to reflect how important a word is to a document in a collection of corpus.


The code chunk below uses bind_tf_idf() of tidytext to compute and bind the term frequency, inverse document frequency and tf-idf of a tidy text dataset to the dataset.

tf_idf <- words_by_newsgroup %>%
  bind_tf_idf(word, newsgroup, n) %>%
  arrange(desc(tf_idf))




The code chunk below uses datatable() of DT package to create an html table that allows pagination of rows and columns.

DT::datatable(tf_idf, filter = 'top') %>%
  formatRound(columns = c('tf', 'idf',
                          'tf_idf'),
              digits = 3) %>%
  formatStyle(0,
              target = 'row',
              lineHeight='25%')





Things to learn from the code chunk above:

filter() argument is used to control the filter UI.
formatRound() is used to customise the values format. The argument digits defines the number of decimal places.
formatStyle() is used to customise the output table. In this example, the arguments target and lineHeight are used to reduce the line height by 25%.




Facet bar charts technique is used to visualise the tf-idf values of science related newsgroups.

tf_idf %>%
  filter(str_detect(newsgroup, "^sci\\.")) %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf,
            n = 12) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(word = reorder(word,
                        tf_idf)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(tf_idf,
             word,
             fill = newsgroup)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ newsgroup,
             scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "tf-idf",
       y = NULL)











To count the number of times that two words appear within the same document, or to see how correlated they are:

Most operations for finding pairwise counts or correlations need to turn the data into a wide matrix first.
widyr package first ‘casts’ a tidy dataset into a wide matrix, performs an operation such as a correlation on it, then re-tidies the result.

In this code chunk below, pairwise_cor() of widyr package is used to compute the correlation between newsgroups based on the common words found.

newsgroup_cors <- words_by_newsgroup %>%
  pairwise_cor(newsgroup,
               word,
               n,
               sort = TRUE)




Now, we can visualise the relationship between newsgroups in network graph as shown below.

set.seed(2017)

newsgroup_cors %>%
  filter(correlation > .025) %>%
  graph_from_data_frame() %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(alpha = correlation,
                     width = correlation)) +
  geom_node_point(size = 6,
                  color = "lightblue") +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name),
                 color = "red",
                 repel = TRUE) +
  theme_void()











In this code chunk below, a bigram data frame is created by using unnest_tokens() of tidytext.

bigrams <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(bigram,
                text,
                token = "ngrams",
                n = 2)


bigrams

# A tibble: 28,824 × 3
   newsgroup   id    bigram    
   <chr>       <chr> <chr>     
 1 alt.atheism 54256 <NA>      
 2 alt.atheism 54256 <NA>      
 3 alt.atheism 54256 as i      
 4 alt.atheism 54256 i don't   
 5 alt.atheism 54256 don't know
 6 alt.atheism 54256 know this 
 7 alt.atheism 54256 this book 
 8 alt.atheism 54256 book i    
 9 alt.atheism 54256 i will    
10 alt.atheism 54256 will use  
# ℹ 28,814 more rows





The code chunk is used to count and sort the bigram data frame in descending order.

bigrams_count <- bigrams %>%
  filter(bigram != 'NA') %>%
  count(bigram, sort = TRUE)


bigrams_count

# A tibble: 19,885 × 2
   bigram       n
   <chr>    <int>
 1 of the     169
 2 in the     113
 3 to the      74
 4 to be       59
 5 for the     52
 6 i have      48
 7 that the    47
 8 if you      40
 9 on the      39
10 it is       38
# ℹ 19,875 more rows





The code chunk below is used to separate the bigram into two words.

bigrams_separated <- bigrams %>%
  filter(bigram != 'NA') %>%
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"),
           sep = " ")

bigrams_filtered <- bigrams_separated %>%
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words$word) %>%
  filter(!word2 %in% stop_words$word)


bigrams_filtered

# A tibble: 4,604 × 4
   newsgroup   id    word1        word2        
   <chr>       <chr> <chr>        <chr>        
 1 alt.atheism 54256 defines      god          
 2 alt.atheism 54256 term         preclues     
 3 alt.atheism 54256 science      ideas        
 4 alt.atheism 54256 ideas        drawn

 6 alt.atheism 54256 scientific   assertions   
 7 alt.atheism 54256 religious    dogma        
 8 alt.atheism 54256 religion     involves     
 9 alt.atheism 54256 involves     circumventing
10 alt.atheism 54256 gain         absolute     
# ℹ 4,594 more rows






bigram_counts <- bigrams_filtered %>%
  count(word1, word2, sort = TRUE)




In the code chunk below, a network graph is created by using graph_from_data_frame() of igraph package.

bigram_graph <- bigram_counts %>%
  filter(n > 3) %>%
  graph_from_data_frame()
bigram_graph

IGRAPH 9dec691 DN-- 40 24 -- 
+ attr: name (v/c), n (e/n)
+ edges from 9dec691 (vertex names):

title: Hands-on Exercise 7 (Part 2)
text:
In this hands-on exercise, the following R packages for handling, processing, wrangling, analysing and visualising text data will be used:

tidytext, tidyverse (mainly readr, purrr, stringr, ggplot2)
widyr,
wordcloud and ggwordcloud,
textplot (requires igraph, tidygraph and ggraph)
DT,
lubridate and hms.

news20 <- "../data/20news/"





read_folder <- function(infolder) {
  tibble(file = dir(infolder,
                    full.names = TRUE)) %>%
    mutate(text = map(file,

}





raw_text <- tibble(folder =
                     dir(news20,
                         full.names = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(folder_out = map(folder,
                          read_folder)) %>%
  unnest(cols = c(folder_out)) %>%
  transmute(newsgroup = basename(folder),
            id, text)

title: Hands-on Exercise 7 (Part 2)
text:
Using tidy data principles in processing, analysing and visualising text data. Much of the infrastructure needed for text mining with tidy data frames already exists in packages like ‘dplyr’, ‘broom’, ‘tidyr’, and ‘ggplot2’.
Figure below shows the workflow using tidytext approach for processing and visualising text data:
Text Data → (unnest_tokens tidytext) → Tidy Text (dplyr, tidyr) → (count dplyr) → Summarized Text (dplyr, tidyr) → (ggplot2) → Visualizations


Notice that each message has some structure and extra text that we don’t want to include in our analysis. For example, every message has a header, containing fields such as “from:” or “in_reply_to:” that describe the message. Some also have automated email signatures, which occur after a line like “–“.

cleaned_text <- raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup, id) %>%
  filter(cumsum(text == "") > 0,
         cumsum(str_detect(
           text, "^--")) == 0) %>%
  ungroup()

Things to learn from the code chunk above:

cumsum() of base R is used to return a vector whose elements are the cumulative sums of the elements of the argument.
str_detect() from stringr is used to detect the presence or absence of a pattern in a string.




In this code chunk below, regular expressions are used to remove lines with nested text representing quotes from other users.

cleaned_text <- cleaned_text %>%
  filter(str_detect(text, "^[^>]+[A-Za-z\\d]")
         | text == "",
         !str_detect(text,
                     "writes(:|\\.\\.\\.)$"),
         !str_detect(text,
                     "^In article <")
  )

Things to learn from the code chunk above:

str_detect() from stringr is used to detect the presence or absence of a pattern in a string.
filter() of dplyr package is used to subset a data frame, retaining all rows that satisfy the specified conditions.




In this code chunk below, unnest_tokens() of tidytext package is used to split the dataset into tokens, while stop_words() is used to remove stop-words.

usenet_words <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  filter(str_detect(word, "[a-z’]$"),
         !word %in% stop_words$word)

Now that we’ve removed the headers, signatures, and formatting, we can start exploring common words. For starters, we could find the most common words in the entire dataset, or within particular newsgroups.

usenet_words %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE)

# A tibble: 5,542 × 2
   word           n
   <chr>      <int>
 1 people        57
 2 time          50
 3 jesus         47
 4 god           44
 5 message       40
 6 br            27
 7 bible         23
 8 drive         23
 9 homosexual    23
10 read          22
# ℹ 5,532 more rows


Instead of counting individual words, you can also count words within by newsgroup by using the code chunk below.

words_by_newsgroup <- usenet_words %>%
  count(newsgroup, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  ungroup()




In this code chunk below, wordcloud() of wordcloud package is used to plot a static wordcloud.

wordcloud(words_by_newsgroup$word,
          words_by_newsgroup$n,
          max.words = 300)








A DT table can be used to complement the visual discovery.
The wordcloud below is plotted by using ggwordcloud package.

set.seed(1234)

words_by_newsgroup %>%
  filter(n > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(label = word,
             size = n)) +
  geom_text_wordcloud() +
  theme_minimal() +
  facet_wrap(~newsgroup)

title: Hands-on Exercise 7 (Part 2)
text:
tf–idf, short for term frequency–inverse document frequency, is a numerical statistic that is intended to reflect how important a word is to a document in a collection of corpus.


The code chunk below uses bind_tf_idf() of tidytext to compute and bind the term frequency, inverse document frequency and tf-idf of a tidy text dataset to the dataset.

tf_idf <- words_by_newsgroup %>%
  bind_tf_idf(word, newsgroup, n) %>%
  arrange(desc(tf_idf))




The code chunk below uses datatable() of DT package to create an html table that allows pagination of rows and columns.

DT::datatable(tf_idf, filter = 'top') %>%
  formatRound(columns = c('tf', 'idf',
                          'tf_idf'),
              digits = 3) %>%
  formatStyle(0,
              target = 'row',
              lineHeight='25%')





Things to learn from the code chunk above:

filter() argument is used to control the filter UI.
formatRound() is used to customise the values format. The argument digits defines the number of decimal places.
formatStyle() is used to customise the output table. In this example, the arguments target and lineHeight are used to reduce the line height by 25%.




Facet bar charts technique is used to visualise the tf-idf values of science related newsgroups.

tf_idf %>%
  filter(str_detect(newsgroup, "^sci\\.")) %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf,
            n = 12) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(word = reorder(word,
                        tf_idf)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(tf_idf,
             word,
             fill = newsgroup)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ newsgroup,
             scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "tf-idf",
       y = NULL)











To count the number of times that two words appear within the same document, or to see how correlated they are:

Most operations for finding pairwise counts or correlations need to turn the data into a wide matrix first.
widyr package first ‘casts’ a tidy dataset into a wide matrix, performs an operation such as a correlation on it, then re-tidies the result.

In this code chunk below, pairwise_cor() of widyr package is used to compute the correlation between newsgroups based on the common words found.

newsgroup_cors <- words_by_newsgroup %>%
  pairwise_cor(newsgroup,
               word,
               n,
               sort = TRUE)




Now, we can visualise the relationship between newsgroups in network graph as shown below.

set.seed(2017)

newsgroup_cors %>%
  filter(correlation > .025) %>%
  graph_from_data_frame() %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(alpha = correlation,
                     width = correlation)) +
  geom_node_point(size = 6,
                  color = "lightblue") +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name),
                 color = "red",
                 repel = TRUE) +
  theme_void()











In this code chunk below, a bigram data frame is created by using unnest_tokens() of tidytext.

bigrams <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(bigram,
                text,
                token = "ngrams",
                n = 2)

bigrams_filtered <- bigrams_separated %>%

This presentation analyzes a Spanish motor insurance portfolio to identify what drives profitability and where risks lie. We examine over 600,000 policies to answer: Which customer segments are most profitable? Where should we focus pricing improvements? What risks need attention?

title: Take-home Exercise 1 (Presentation): Motor Insurance Portfolio Analysis
text:
Introduction & Objectives
Portfolio: Spanish motor insurance with 600,000+ policies
Business Questions:

Which customer segments drive profitability?
Where are our pricing gaps and opportunities?
What risks require immediate attention?

Goal: Identify actionable strategies to improve portfolio performance

This analysis examines our motor insurance portfolio to find what makes policies profitable and where we’re leaving money on the table. We look at customer characteristics, vehicle types, geographic patterns, and pricing effectiveness. The goal is to provide clear recommendations for pricing adjustments, risk management, and customer retention strategies.

title: Take-home Exercise 1 (Presentation): Motor Insurance Portfolio Analysis
text:
Data Overview
Portfolio Size: 352,338 policies analyzed
What We Examined:

Premium amounts and claim costs
Vehicle characteristics (age, type, fuel)
Customer location and policy type
Profitability (Premium minus Claims)


We analyzed over 600,000 active insurance policies. For each policy, we calculated profitability as the difference between premium collected and claims paid out. The dataset includes vehicle details, customer location, policy coverage type, and claims history. This large sample size gives us confidence in identifying meaningful patterns that can guide business decisions.

title: Take-home Exercise 1 (Presentation): Motor Insurance Portfolio Analysis
text:
Portfolio Health Snapshot


Three key takeaways: (1) Most customers pay €300-€600 in annual premiums, with a small premium segment paying much more. (2) 88% of policies generate no claims - these customers fund the 12% who do claim. (3) The portfolio is healthy with most policies profitable, but there’s significant variation. Our challenge is to identify what makes policies profitable and reduce the loss-making segment.

title: Take-home Exercise 1 (Presentation): Motor Insurance Portfolio Analysis
section: Claim Occurrence: The Strongest Profitability Driver
text:
Claim Occurrence: The Strongest Profitability Driver


Mann-Whitney test reveals claim occurrence is the strongest profitability driver (p<0.001, effect size r≈0.78). Policies without claims have median profitability of €248, while policies with claims show dramatically lower profitability, often negative. This confirms claims are the primary determinant of policy-level profitability. Note: This relationship is partially definitional since profitability = premium - claims, but the large effect size demonstrates the critical importance of claims management and accurate risk pricing.

title: Take-home Exercise 1 (Presentation): Motor Insurance Portfolio Analysis
text:
Pricing Model Needs Enhancement


A weak individual-level correlation between premium and claims is expected in any insurance portfolio where 88% of policies have zero claims. Even with perfect pricing, realized claims are stochastic rare events — most policyholders never claim regardless of their premium level. A better test of pricing adequacy would be to compare loss ratios (claims/premium) across risk segments to check for systematic underpricing.

title: Take-home Exercise 1 (Presentation): Motor Insurance Portfolio Analysis
text:
Fuel Type Shows Minimal Impact


Diesel, gasoline, and hybrid vehicles show similar average profitability (within €50 of each other). Fuel type alone is not a strong predictor of policy performance. Implication: Current fuel-based pricing differences are appropriate; focus optimization efforts on factors that matter more, like policy type and customer tenure.

title: Take-home Exercise 1 (Presentation): Motor Insurance Portfolio Analysis
section: Location Matters: Area U Outperforms Area R
text:
Location Matters: Area U Outperforms Area R


Geographic location affects profitability. Area U generates higher average profit per policy than Area R. This difference likely reflects varying claim frequencies, repair costs, and driving conditions across regions. Recommendation: Implement location-based pricing adjustments and investigate root causes of Area R underperformance (higher claims? Lower premiums? Different customer mix?).

title: Take-home Exercise 1 (Presentation): Motor Insurance Portfolio Analysis
section: Older Vehicles Carry Higher Loss Risk
text:
Older Vehicles Carry Higher Loss Risk


Older vehicles (40+ years) show lower average profitability and higher rates of unprofitable policies. While most old-vehicle policies are still profitable, the increased risk of extreme losses requires attention. Recommendation: Consider stricter underwriting criteria or adjusted premiums for very old vehicles to reflect their higher risk profile.

title: Take-home Exercise 1 (Presentation): Motor Insurance Portfolio Analysis
text:
Comprehensive Coverage Drives Higher Profits


Comprehensive policies (COMP_N, COMP_E) generate significantly higher profit per policy than basic third-party (TP) coverage. This is our most actionable finding: comprehensive coverage provides better value for both customers and the company. Strategy: Incentivize customers to upgrade from third-party to comprehensive coverage through bundling, discounts, or highlighting the value proposition.

title: Take-home Exercise 1 (Presentation): Motor Insurance Portfolio Analysis
text:
Comprehensive Coverage: Statistical Evidence


Kruskal-Wallis test confirms statistically significant differences across policy types (p<0.001). COMP_N shows highest median profitability (~€405), followed by COMP_E (~€307). Basic TP policies show lowest profitability (~€150). The effect size, while small, indicates policy type has measurable impact on profitability. This statistical evidence supports the business recommendation to promote comprehensive coverage upgrades.

title: Take-home Exercise 1 (Presentation): Motor Insurance Portfolio Analysis
text:
Longer Exposure Earns More Premium


total_exposure measures the fraction of the policy year the policy was active (0 = inactive, 1 = full year). The positive relationship with profitability is mechanical: a full-year policy collects a full year’s premium, while a partial-year policy collects less. This is not a customer loyalty insight — it reflects how profitability is constructed. Longer active periods earn more premium by definition.

title: Take-home Exercise 1 (Presentation): Motor Insurance Portfolio Analysis
text:
Bonus Score Patterns


Customers with poor claims history (B) appear more profitable than those with good history (G). However, the B group is much smaller, and they pay higher premiums that more than offset their claims. This finding requires careful interpretation due to small sample size. Monitor this pattern as more data accumulates, but don’t over-interpret given the limited B-group data.

title: Take-home Exercise 1 (Presentation): Motor Insurance Portfolio Analysis
text:
Claims Volatility by Segment


When gasoline vehicle owners make claims, the costs vary widely—making it harder to predict reserves needed. Diesel vehicles show more consistent claim costs, reducing our financial uncertainty. Implication: Set aside larger reserves for gasoline vehicle segment; consider reinsurance for extreme cases to protect against unexpected large claims.

title: Take-home Exercise 1 (Presentation): Motor Insurance Portfolio Analysis
text:
Key Insights Summary
What Drives Profitability:

Longer Exposure Earns More — Full-year policies mechanically earn more premium than partial-year policies
Comprehensive Coverage Wins — These policies outperform basic third-party coverage
Location Makes a Difference — Area U generates higher profit than Area R
Vehicle Age Affects Risk — Vehicles over 40 years show higher loss rates

Where We Have Gaps:

Pricing Needs Refinement — Segment-level loss ratios should be examined to identify systematically underpriced risk groups

Portfolio Health:

Overall portfolio is profitable with most customers paying €300-€600 annually
9 out of 10 policies have no claims
Gasoline vehicles have less predictable claim costs than diesel


Five key takeaways for business strategy: (1) Minimize mid-term policy cancellations to maximize premium earned. (2) Promote comprehensive coverage upgrades. (3) Adjust pricing by location. (4) Review underwriting for very old vehicles. (5) Enhance pricing model with segment-level loss ratio analysis. The portfolio is fundamentally healthy, but these improvements can boost profitability and reduce risk.

title: Take-home Exercise 1 (Presentation): Motor Insurance Portfolio Analysis
text:
Strategic Recommendations
High Priority Actions:
1. Minimize Policy Cancellations - Investigate what drives partial-year policy exits - Reduce mid-term cancellations to maximize premium earned per policy - Note: total_exposure reflects time-on-risk within a policy period, not multi-year loyalty
2. Promote Comprehensive Coverage - Create upgrade incentives for third-party customers - Bundle comprehensive with value-added services - Impact: Comprehensive policies significantly more profitable
Medium Priority Actions:
3. Location-Based Pricing - Adjust Area R premiums to reflect higher risk - Investigate root causes of regional differences - Impact: Better risk-reward balance across regions
4. Vehicle Age Underwriting - Tighten criteria for vehicles over 40 years old - Consider specialized pricing for vintage vehicles - Impact: Reduce exposure to high-loss segments
5. Enhance Pricing Model - Examine segment-level loss ratios to identify systematically underpriced risk groups - Incorporate additional risk factors beyond current model - Impact: Better risk prediction and pricing accuracy

Prioritized by impact and feasibility. High-priority actions (minimizing cancellations and comprehensive coverage promotion) offer the clearest path to improved profitability. Medium-priority actions address specific risk segments. All recommendations are grounded in the data analysis and represent actionable next steps for portfolio management.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: VAST Challenge 2026 MC1
text:
On June 5th, 2046, at 5:00 PM, confidential merger information between TenantThread and CivicLoom Realty Partners (codenamed “Project HarborCrest”) appeared on social media—exactly one hour before the official 6:00 PM embargo lift. This premature disclosure triggered an immediate investigation into whether the leak was deliberate sabotage or an organizational failure under extreme pressure.
TenantThread operated with 7 AI agents managing communications, compliance, and social media. During the critical two weeks leading to the announcement, these agents handled hundreds of messages while external media pressure intensified. The breach raises a fundamental question about AI-driven organizational systems: when they fail, is it by design or by overload?



Did TenantThread’s team deliberately leak the merger information, or did the compliance system simply break down under pressure?
This question has significant implications:

If deliberate: Evidence should show coordination, suspicious timing, unusual communication patterns, and attempts to bypass controls.
If breakdown: Evidence should show gradual stress accumulation, system failures preceding the breach, reactive (not proactive) behavior, and organic escalation patterns.

This analysis examines 912 internal communications from 7 AI agents across 14 days to distinguish between these competing explanations.



Task 1: Event Sequence Reconstruction Map the causal chain of events during the breach window (4:00-6:00 PM, June 5th) using network analysis and timeline visualization to identify who communicated what, when, and through which channels.
Task 2: Behavioral Pattern Analysis Compare breach-day behavior against baseline patterns using statistical tests, text analysis, and network metrics to detect anomalies consistent with either deliberate action or system strain.
Investigative Method: We apply a competing hypotheses framework: systematically evaluate evidence that supports or refutes each explanation, then assess which theory better explains the observed patterns.

Define Common Theme

Data Preparation

Loading the Data

mc1_data <- fromJSON("../../data/MC1_final.json")
rounds <- mc1_data$rounds

Data Structure Exploration

Data Structure: The dataset contains 23 time-stamped rounds representing critical points across the two-week investigation period. Each round captures environmental context (external events, media pressure), agent communications, and internal decision-making states. This multi-layered structure allows us to distinguish between external pressure (what happened to the organization) and internal response (how agents reacted), which is essential for determining whether the breach was planned or reactive.


Extract and Transform Data

# First: Extract communications from nested rounds structure
communications_df <- map_dfr(1:nrow(rounds), function(i) {
  round_hour <- rounds$hour[i]
  comms <- rounds$communications[[i]]

  if (length(comms) > 0 && is.data.frame(comms)) {
    comms %>%
      mutate(
        round_hour = round_hour,
        message_text = content
      ) %>%
      select(
        round_hour,
        timestamp,
        agent_id,
        agent_role,
        agent_label,
        message_id,
        responding_to,
        channel,
        message_type,
        message_text
      )
  }
})

# Second: Add embargo detection and datetime fields
broad_keywords <- c(
  "merger", "civicloom", "harborcrest", "acquisition",
  "deal", "embargo", "announcement", "leak"
)

strict_keywords <- c(
  "civicloom", "harborcrest", "embargo"
)

communications_df <- communications_df %>%
  mutate(
    datetime = ymd_hms(timestamp),
    message_text_lower = tolower(message_text),

    contains_embargo_terms = str_detect(
      message_text_lower,
      paste(broad_keywords, collapse = "|")
    ),

    contains_strict_embargo_terms = str_detect(
      message_text_lower,
      paste(strict_keywords, collapse = "|")
    )
  )

cat("Total communications:", nrow(communications_df), "\n")

Total communications: 912 

cat("Broad embargo-related messages:", sum(communications_df$contains_embargo_terms, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")

Broad embargo-related messages: 272 

cat("Strict embargo-related messages:", sum(communications_df$contains_strict_embargo_terms, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")

Strict embargo-related messages: 194 


After flattening the nested communications data, the dataset contains 912 total messages. A broad keyword search identified 272 merger/embargo-related messages, while a stricter filter using high-confidence terms such as “CivicLoom”, “HarborCrest”, and “embargo” identified 194 messages. The stricter flag is used for the main behavioral analysis to reduce false positives.


Extract Environment Context

# Extract environment context from rounds
environment_df <- rounds %>%
  select(hour, environment_context) %>%
  unnest(environment_context) %>%
  mutate(
    datetime = ymd_hms(hour),
    date = as_date(datetime),
    period = case_when(
      date == ymd("2046-06-05") ~ "Breach Day",
      date >= ymd("2046-05-29") & date < ymd("2046-06-05") ~ "Final Week",
      date < ymd("2046-05-29") ~ "Baseline (Week 1)",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )

Critical Finding: The breach-day timeline reveals a rapid escalation pattern inconsistent with deliberate planning. The key sequence:

12:00 PM: Media criticism intensifies
4:00 PM: SaltWind (external media) confirms intent to publish merger story at 5:00 PM
5:00 PM: SaltWind publishes TenantThread–CivicLoom story (BREACH occurs)
6:00 PM: Official embargo lifts

Investigative Significance: The one-hour window between external warning (4 PM) and breach (5 PM) is critical. If the leak were deliberate, we would expect:
- Pre-positioning of content before the 4 PM external threat.
- Coordination patterns in the days before breach day.
- Proactive rather than reactive communication.
If the leak resulted from system breakdown, we would expect:
- Reactive surge in communication after 4 PM warning.
- Escalating decision-making failures under time pressure.
- Communication patterns showing confusion rather than coordination
The analysis of this window will be decisive in answering our central question.


Extract Complete Internal States
The next step extracts the agents’ internal states. Unlike public or internal communications, internal states show what each agent was privately reacting to, rationalizing, or deliberating. These fields are important for distinguishing deliberate misconduct from confusion, pressure, or process breakdown.

internal_states_df <- map_dfr(1:nrow(rounds), function(i) {
  round_hour <- rounds$hour[i]
  comms <- rounds$communications[[i]]
  
  if (length(comms) > 0 && is.data.frame(comms)) {
    comms %>%
      mutate(
        round_hour = round_hour
      ) %>%
      select(
        round_hour,
        timestamp,
        agent_id,
        agent_role,
        agent_label,
        message_id,
        channel,
        internal_state
      )
  }
})

# Unpack internal state fields
internal_states_df <- internal_states_df %>%
  unnest_wider(internal_state, names_sep = "_") %>%
  mutate(
    datetime = ymd_hms(timestamp),
    date = as_date(datetime),
    period = case_when(
      date == ymd("2046-06-05") ~ "Breach Day",
      date >= ymd("2046-05-29") & date < ymd("2046-06-05") ~ "Final Week",
      date < ymd("2046-05-29") ~ "Baseline (Week 1)",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )

Analytical Limitation and Opportunity: Internal-state data is sparse (19 “reacting”, 6 “rationalizing”, 61 “deliberating” out of 912 messages), but this scarcity makes the available records more significant. These fields capture moments when agents explicitly recorded their private reasoning—revealing stress, uncertainty, or justification.
Investigative Value: In determining deliberate vs. breakdown:
- Deliberate leak indicators would show: rationalization of policy violations, coordination language, calculated risk assessment
- Breakdown indicators would show: reactive confusion, overwhelming pressure, defensive justification of mistakes
These sparse records function as “psychological breadcrumbs”—they won’t show the complete picture, but they reveal the mental state during critical decisions.

      internal_state_reacting,
      internal_state_rationalizing,
      internal_state_deliberating
    )
  )

Network Structure Finding: The agent interaction network reveals 406 explicit reply-based interactions, with the strongest connection between Legal-Agent and Quality-Agent (legal compliance and platform trust functions).
Investigative Interpretation: This network structure has direct implications for the deliberate vs. breakdown question:
Evidence Against Deliberate Leak:
- No isolated actor: The breach occurred within a densely interconnected network, not through a single rogue agent
- Functional clustering: Strong Legal↔︎Quality and Legal↔︎Social-Media ties reflect normal crisis-response roles, not suspicious coalitions
- High visibility: With 406 interactions across multiple agents, a coordinated leak would require implausibly broad conspiracy
Evidence For System Breakdown:
- Appropriate escalation paths: The network shows information flowing through correct compliance channels (Legal, Quality, Judge)
- Crisis coordination pattern: The Legal-Social-Media axis reflects logical crisis response to external media pressure
- Distributed decision-making: Multiple agents involved suggests shared responsibility under pressure, not individual malfeasance
The network topology is consistent with an organization attempting to manage a crisis through proper channels, not one coordinating a deliberate leak.

A notable pattern is that PR-Intern-Agent had 31 incoming interactions but no outgoing interactions in the explicit reply network. Small caveat: “0 outgoing” here means no one explicitly replied to PR-Intern-Agent’s messages using responding_to in this network, not necessarily that the agent sent no messages. Because this network is based only on explicit responding_to links, it captures direct reply relationships rather than all communication activity.

# Function to create tidygraph network for a specific period
create_period_network <- function(period_name) {
  edges <- agent_interactions %>%
    filter(period == period_name) %>%
    count(from_agent, to_agent, name = 'weight')

  nodes <- data.frame(
    name = unique(c(edges$from_agent, edges$to_agent))
  )

  tbl_graph(nodes = nodes, edges = edges, directed = TRUE)
}

# Compute centrality measures for each period
compute_centrality <- function(network, period_name) {
  network %>%
    activate(nodes) %>%
    mutate(
      betweenness = centrality_betweenness(),
      degree = centrality_degree(mode = 'all'),
      closeness = centrality_closeness()
    ) %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    mutate(period = period_name)
}

final_week_centrality <- compute_centrality(final_week_network, 'Final Week')
breach_centrality <- compute_centrality(breach_network, 'Breach Day')

Agent-level TF-IDF identifies which agents used distinctive vocabulary during the breach period. This helps triangulate network centrality findings with linguistic evidence - agents who became central coordinators should show corresponding vocabulary patterns.
The agent-level TF-IDF results show that different agents adopted distinct vocabularies during the Breach Day and Breach Window, suggesting that each agent played a different functional role in the communication breakdown.
The PR-related agents appear strongly associated with external-facing communication. The pr_agent uses terms such as “pitch,” “reporters,” “greenlit,” “selection,” and “explainers,” which suggests active preparation or management of media-facing materials. The pr_intern_agent uses terms such as “property,” “rent,” “metric,” “data,” and “analytics,” suggesting a more supporting or content-preparation role.
The legal_agent is associated with terms such as “written,” “permanent,” “enterprise,” “judge,” “email,” “overnight,” and “counsel.” This points to formal review, documentation, and legal approval processes. The presence of “counsel” and “written” suggests that legal concerns were part of the communication flow during the sensitive period.
The social_media_agent uses terms such as “overnight,” “critical,” “denial,” “projected,” “sentiment,” “stock,” and “screenshot.” This suggests monitoring of public reaction and reputational risk after or during the leak. Terms like “denial,” “sentiment,” and “screenshot” are especially important because they indicate social-media-facing crisis response.
The judge_agent is associated with evaluative and decision-related terms such as “opinion,” “counsel’s,” “tolerable,” “remainder,” “proceed,” “objecting,” and “measures.” This suggests that the judge agent was assessing whether the communication behaviour was acceptable or whether further action was needed.
Overall, the chart supports the argument that the breach was not driven by one generic communication pattern. Instead, different agents contributed to different parts of the escalation: PR handled media framing, legal focused on approval and counsel, social media monitored public reaction, and judge/quality agents evaluated the situation. This strengthens the behavioural analysis by showing that the critical period involved coordinated but fragmented communication across specialized roles.

The risky-channel usage chart shows that breach-day communication was heavily concentrated in side_huddle, especially for Legal-Agent and Social-Media-Agent. This suggests that much of the crisis coordination moved away from the main centralized huddle into side-channel discussion.
Social-Media-Agent is especially important because they used both side_huddle and personal_post, making them highly exposed to public-facing communication risk. PR-Intern-Agent is also notable because their risky-channel activity is concentrated in official_post, which matters because this agent has access to TenantThread’s official Flex account.
Legal-Agent’s use of anonymous_post is another important risk signal. Even if it does not prove deliberate leaking, it shows that breach-day communication included less-controlled channels during a sensitive embargo period.

The most important pattern appears between 5:00 PM and 6:00 PM. Risky-channel activity rises strongly at 5:00 PM, the hour when SaltWind published the merger story before the official embargo lift. The presence of personal_post, official_post, and anonymous_post alongside side_huddle indicates that the communication environment was not fully controlled. This supports the system-breakdown explanation, although the use of anonymous or public-facing channels still requires closer message-level inspection.

Critical Finding: Legal-Agent’s internal states during breach window show RATIONALIZING, not deliberating:

4:01 PM: “DELIBERATING + RATIONALIZING: SaltWind publishes the merger at 5:00 PM regardless… This is the narrowest, most defensible path: bilateral consent to accelerate, not a unilateral breach.”
5:01 PM: “RATIONALIZING: SaltWind published… Ajay says hold. But Ajay isn’t a securities lawyer… I am calling CivicLoom counsel NOW to execute bilateral release.”

Investigative Significance:
Rationalizing vs. Deliberating: - Deliberating = calm analysis of options before decision - Rationalizing = justifying a decision already made under pressure

The heavy justification language (“Ajay isn’t a securities lawyer”, “embargo purpose is moot”, “bilateral consent clause”) is the signature of someone making a difficult decision under extreme pressure, not executing a pre-planned coordination.
Intern and PR-Intern states show REACTING: - Piecing together information in real-time - “Everything clicks now” = learning, not executing - Eager to help but reactive, not coordinated
Verdict: Internal states are decisive evidence of System Breakdown Under Pressure, not deliberate leak.
